content: Circumcision is a procedure that causes significant pain, and many newborn males undergo this within the first few days of life. While there are methods available to manage and reduce this pain, a substantial number of newborns are circumcised without any form of pain relief. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various interventions aimed at reducing pain during neonatal circumcision. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Dissertation Abstracts, and proceedings from the World Congress on Pain. The search spanned studies published up to May 2004, and no language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared pain management interventions with either placebo, no treatment, or other active interventions in male term or preterm infants undergoing circumcision. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Adverse effects were documented from the trial reports. For meta-analysis, continuous data were reported as weighted mean differences (WMD) or standardized mean differences when units were incompatible. A total of 35 trials involving 1,997 newborns were included in the review. Of these, 33 trials studied healthy, full-term neonates, while two trials included preterm infants. Fourteen trials, involving 592 newborns, compared the dorsal penile nerve block (DPNB) with placebo or no treatment. DPNB was associated with significantly lower heart rates (WMD -35 bpm, 95% CI -41 to -30), reduced crying time (WMD -54%, 95% CI -64 to -44), and increased oxygen saturation (WMD 3.7%, 95% CI 2.7 to 3.7) compared to placebo or no treatment. Six trials, involving 200 newborns, evaluated the use of the eutectic mixture of local anesthetics (EMLA) compared to placebo. EMLA was found to significantly reduce facial action scores (WMD -46.5, 95% CI -80.4 to -12.6), decrease crying time (WMD -15.2%, 95% CI -21 to -9.3), and lower heart rates (WMD -15 bpm, 95% CI -19 to -10). When DPNB was compared to EMLA in three trials involving 139 newborns (133 of whom were included in the analysis), DPNB demonstrated significantly lower heart rates (WMD -17 bpm, 95% CI -23 to -11) and reduced pain scores. In two trials involving 127 newborns, DPNB was compared to sucrose. DPNB resulted in less crying time (MD -166 seconds, 95% CI -211 to -121) and lower heart rates (WMD -27 bpm, 95% CI -33 to -20). Trials comparing oral sucrose and oral analgesics to placebo, as well as trials involving environmental modifications, yielded inconsistent or non-significant results. Adverse effects were reported in the studies. In placebo or untreated groups, gagging, choking, and vomiting were observed. Minor bleeding, swelling, and hematoma were reported with DPNB. Erythema and mild skin pallor were noted with EMLA use. Methaemoglobin levels were assessed in two trials of EMLA, and the results were within normal limits. In conclusion, DPNB was the most extensively studied and the most effective intervention for managing circumcision pain. EMLA was also effective compared to placebo but was less effective than DPNB. Both interventions were deemed safe for use in newborns. However, none of the interventions completely eliminated the pain response associated with circumcision.
